planting.note: Let cut stems callus for one to two weeks before setting them in fast-draining, sandy soil in full sun after the last frost.

directions: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining, sandy or gritty soil in full sun, watering only lightly until new roots and leaves appear. Divine produces very large, heavily textured flowers with broad cream-white petals warming to a deep golden throat, carrying one of the strongest, sweetest fragrances of any named plumeria and making it a favorite for lei-making in Hawaii. Like other deciduous Plumeria rubra selections, it drops its leaves and goes dormant in cool weather, so watering should be cut back sharply through winter to avoid stem and root rot. Keep it frost-free year-round, moving container specimens indoors or into a greenhouse anywhere winter temperatures approach freezing.

common_name: Dean Conklin Plumeria (Fragrant Deep Red Frangipani)

planting.note: Allow cuttings to callus for one to two weeks before planting in well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F.

directions: Dean Conklin bears rounded clusters of deep wine-red to burgundy flowers with a velvety texture and a strong, sweet fragrance, one of the darkest-colored named plumeria widely grown by collectors. Root cuttings in fast-draining, sandy soil in full sun and withhold heavy watering until new growth confirms rooting has begun. The plant is deciduous and rests leafless through the cool season, so irrigation should be minimal in winter to prevent stem and root rot. Protect it from any frost and bring container plants under cover whenever temperatures threaten to drop near freezing.

common_name: King Kalakaua Plumeria (Fragrant Multicolor Hawaiian Frangipani)

planting.note: Root callused cuttings in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun after the last frost, once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm.

directions: Named for the last reigning king of the Kingdom of Hawaii, King Kalakaua produces large, wide-petaled flowers blending yellow, pink, and white tones with a rich, classic frangipani scent. Propagate from stem cuttings callused for one to two weeks before setting them in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun. Reduce watering sharply once the plant drops its leaves for winter dormancy, since wet soil around a leafless plumeria in cool weather is the most common cause of stem rot. Give it full sun and complete frost protection, as it has no cold hardiness outside the warmest tropical and subtropical zones.

common_name: Prince of Orange Ixora (Color-Changing Orange Flame-of-the-Woods)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the heaviest bloom.

directions: Prince of Orange opens clusters of bright orange, star-shaped flowers that gradually deepen to a rosy red-orange as they age, so a single cluster often shows both colors at once. Plant in acidic, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and keep young plants evenly watered while roots establish. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season, since ixora quickly develops yellow, interveinal chlorosis in the alkaline soils common along the Gulf Coast and in South Florida. It has no cold tolerance, so protect it from frost and expect dieback if temperatures drop into the mid-30s or below.

common_name: Min-A-Min Orange Jessamine (Dwarf Compact Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil; this dwarf selection needs far less pruning than seed-grown orange jessamine to stay compact.

directions: Min-A-Min is a naturally dwarf, dense selection of orange jessamine that tops out at two to four feet, far more compact than the eight- to fifteen-foot species, making it useful as a low hedge, foundation planting, or container specimen where full-size Murraya would quickly outgrow the space. It produces the same small, intensely fragrant white star-shaped flowers in repeated flushes through the warm months, followed by small orange-red berries. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain its naturally tidy form. Because Murraya paniculata is a known host for citrus greening disease, check local regulations before purchasing or transporting this cultivar.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Murraya paniculata (Orange Jessamine)
